title: About Me
text:
I am a marine, estuarine, and freshwater biology and sustainability dual major at the University of New Hampshire. I have worked with Dr. Nathan Furey’s Fish and Movement Ecology Lab and Dr. Karolina Kwasek’s Aquaculture Lab here at UNH. I have also helped the Marine Bioacoustics and Behavior Lab with gear deployment and I will be working with the Center for Sustainable Seafood Systems to develop sustainable scallop aquaculture at UNH next semester too. My primary interests lie in studying forage fish ecology and antipredator behavioral responses, but I am also interested in bioacoustics. I enjoy coding in R and am always interested in learning new quantitative methods. I love ice cream, building Legos, listening to music, and watching Formula 1 Racing.

Education
I am a marine, estuarine, and freshwater biology and sustainability dual major at the University of New Hampshire (GPA 3.94). I plan to pursue a MS in Ecology after I graduate in May 2027.

title: Projects
text:
Contributors: Esher Swanson, Kimberly A. Lato, Nathan B. Furey
Forage Fish are important prey for many organisms because they connect and disperse energy across food webs. Higher availability of energy dense forage fish is correlated with higher ecosystem productivity and resilience to ecosystem stressors such as warming. This study collects forage fish samples from seine surveys, dropped prey items at White Island’s tern colony, and directly from the stomach contents of striped bass (Morone saxatilis) and Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua). Samples are dried, homogenized, and pressed into pellets. These pellets are then combusted using a bomb calorimeter to learn how much energy is contained in one gram of sample. Prey species with a higher energy density have higher value to predators, so changes in prey energetics can alter predator foraging effort and food webs.




Contributors: Esher Swanson, Atlas Emmanuel, Sidney Axtell, Nathan B. Furey
Atlantic cod and striped bass are economically and ecologically important generalist predators in Gulf of Maine fisheries. The quality of their diets may affect their capacity to adapt to warming waters. This project collects stomach contents from these species through gastric lavage (nonlethal; stomach flushing) to identify what these predators are eating. Data on prey energetics from project 1 will be coupled with data on prey species abundance from this study to gain a better picture of diet quality.



Contributors: Esher Swanson, Matt Scott, Shae Shandroff, Trevor Banister, Nathan B. Furey
Rainbow smelt are important prey for species such as striped bass (Morone saxatilis), Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua), and Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) while also supporting New Hampshire ice fisheries. The Furey Lab tags smelt to better understand migration and spawning behavior, which offers an opportunity to collect morphometric data and fish scale samples. I clean and age these scales in an effort to assign each fish and its morphometric data to a yearly cohort. Understanding which yearly cohorts had higher growth and survival can then allow us to plot these data alongside environmental data and identify the environmental factors that affect smelt population success.

title: Projects
text:
Dr. Karolina Kwasek’s Aquaculture Lab

Effects of Simulating Natural Environment on Zebrafish (Danio rerio) Growth and Survival
Contributors: Esher Swanson, Simon Laidlaw, Juliana Sanzi, Jessica Robinson, Karolina Kwasek
Past aquaculture studies have shown that increasing environmental complexity can positively impact fish growth and survival in aquaculture. This can take many forms, from adding plants to adding images/actual substrate. The natural habitat of Zebrafish is freshwater floodplains characterized by silt and vegetation, so we are seeing if images of silt and addition of vegetation improves zebrafish growth and survival. Zebrafish are essentially the lab rats of the sea so any improvement in culturing practices could benefit several industries using zebrafish as a model organism.


Replacing Rotifers (Brachionus plicatilis) with Decapsulated Artemia as a Means of Improving Current Zebrafish (Danio rerio) Culture Practices
Contributors: Esher Swanson, Jessica Robinson, Karolina Kwasek
Zebrafish are a vertebrate model organism used for research in many industries, from human health to neurobiology. This study aimed to improve larval rearing practices during which high mortality is typically observed. Rotifers, a common larval feed for zebrafish, are unpredictable and time intensive to culture so this study replaced them with decapsulated Artemia nauplii and tested growth and survival. Results showed zebrafish fed decapsulated Artemia had higher survival and comparable growth. Thus, this study’s experimental feeding regime could become a standardized feeding protocol for raising larval zebrafish.

Development of Scallop Aquaculture
Contributors: Esher Swanson, Lyla Tulloch, Kaitlyn Ilacqua, Emily Kumph, Michael Coogan, Michael Doherty, David Fredrikkson
We will study methods of optimizing sustainable scallop farming in the Gulf of Maine using marine-mammal-safe equipment and create a potential business model.
